name: Apollo 11 Lunar Module (Eagle)
statusDetail: The descent stage remains on the Moon at Tranquility Base. The ascent stage was left in lunar orbit after the crew returned to the command module, and its final fate is not confirmed.
physicalLocation: Moon (descent stage at Tranquility Base, Sea of Tranquility)
purpose: Carry two astronauts from lunar orbit down to the Moon's surface and back up again.
simpleExplanation: A spidery spacecraft that carried two astronauts down to the Moon. Its top half then worked as a rocket to carry them back up, and the bottom half stayed behind.
scientificContribution: Delivered the first humans to the Moon and returned them to lunar orbit, allowing them to collect lunar samples and set up experiments.
historicalSignificance: Eagle made the first crewed landing on another world on July 20, 1969.
modelDescription: A boxy, four-legged lander in two parts: a wide descent stage wrapped in gold-coloured foil with landing legs and a ladder, and a smaller angular ascent stage on top with two triangular windows, antennas and small thrusters.
audioDescription: The Apollo Lunar Module looks like a gold and silver insect standing on four spindly legs, about seven metres tall. The lower half, the descent stage, is a wide, boxy platform wrapped in crinkled gold-coloured foil, with a ladder running down one leg. The upper half, the ascent stage, is a smaller, angular cabin with two triangular windows at the front, like eyes, where the two astronauts stood. Antennas and small rocket thrusters stick out from its sides.
visualExplanation: The lander separated from the main spacecraft in lunar orbit and flew down to the surface. After the Moon walk, only the top half, the ascent stage, fired its engine and lifted off. The bottom half stayed on the Moon and acted as the launch platform.
reviewNotes: Confirm the NSSDCA ID matches Eagle, the ascent-stage fate, and the exact mission end date. Other Apollo landers can be added as separate records.

name: Lunar Roving Vehicle (Apollo 15)
statusDetail: Left on the Moon at the end of the Apollo 15 surface mission. Rovers were also left on the Moon by Apollo 16 and Apollo 17.
purpose: Transport astronauts and their tools across the lunar surface.
simpleExplanation: A battery-powered moon buggy that folded up to fit inside the lander, then unfolded so astronauts could drive across the Moon.
scientificContribution: Let astronauts travel much farther from the lander, carry more equipment and bring back more rock and soil samples.
historicalSignificance: The first car driven on the Moon, used on Apollo 15, 16 and 17.
modelDescription: An open, lightweight frame with four wire-mesh wheels, two side-by-side seats, a T-shaped hand controller, and a mesh dish antenna on a mast at the front.
modelSource: Mondfahrzeug (Lunar Rover)|(https://skfb.ly/otJtA) by Deutsches Museum | Digital is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/).
audioDescription: The Lunar Roving Vehicle is an open, lightweight frame on four wheels, about three metres long. Two bucket seats sit side by side in the middle, with a small T-shaped hand controller between them. At the front, a dish-shaped mesh antenna rises on a mast, with a television camera nearby. The wheels have no solid rubber tyres. They are woven from metal wire, with metal chevrons for grip.
visualExplanation: The rover was stored folded flat on the side of the lander. An astronaut pulled cables to lower it to the ground, and its frame and wheels unfolded into shape. A battery sent power to an electric motor in each wheel.
reviewNotes: Confirm the NSSDCA ID points to the rover record. Confirm landing region and mission end date. Apollo 16 and 17 rovers can be added as separate records.

name: Surveyor 3
statusDetail: Landed on April 20, 1967 in Oceanus Procellarum and stopped operating later that year. Apollo 12 astronauts visited it in November 1969.
purpose: Test soft landing on the Moon and study the lunar surface to prepare for crewed landings.
simpleExplanation: A robot scout that landed on the Moon before any astronaut, taking photos and digging in the soil to check whether the ground was safe.
scientificContribution: Sent back thousands of photographs and used a scoop to test how strong the lunar soil is, helping NASA plan the Apollo landings.
historicalSignificance: Apollo 12 astronauts walked to Surveyor 3 and brought parts of it back to Earth for study.
modelDescription: A three-legged robotic lander with a central mast carrying a camera and a flat solar panel, and a small scoop arm for digging into lunar soil.
modelSource: Surveyor 3 3D model procedurally generated using Python and the trimesh library, based on NASA historical spacecraft specifications.
audioDescription: Surveyor 3 stands on three legs, with a tall, thin aluminium frame like a tripod. A mast rises from the middle, with a flat solar panel on top and a television camera just below it, looking out across the surface. A short robotic arm with a small scoop folds close to the body and can reach out to dig into the soil.
visualExplanation: Surveyor slowed itself with a rocket and landed on three legs. Its camera photographed the surroundings and sent pictures to Earth. Its scoop arm dug small trenches to test how firm the soil was.
reviewNotes: Confirm the last-contact and mission end dates. Surveyors 1, 5, 6 and 7 also landed and can be added as separate records.

name: Sojourner Rover
statusDetail: Operated far longer than planned. Communication with the Pathfinder lander, which relayed the rover's data, ended in September 1997.
purpose: Explore the ground near the Pathfinder lander and study the chemistry of Martian rocks and soil.
simpleExplanation: A tiny six-wheeled robot, about the size of a microwave oven, that drove around on Mars and tested rocks.
scientificContribution: Used an instrument pressed against rocks to measure what they were made of, and showed that a small rover could work on Mars.
historicalSignificance: The first rover to operate on the surface of Mars.
modelDescription: A small, box-shaped rover on six wheels with a flat solar panel on top, a suspension that lets it climb over rocks, and a small instrument for studying rocks.
audioDescription: Sojourner is a small, flat, box-shaped rover about the size of a microwave oven. It rides on six wheels, joined by a rocking suspension that lets it climb over rocks. A dark solar panel covers the top. A small instrument, the alpha proton X-ray spectrometer, could be pressed against rocks to measure what they were made of.
visualExplanation: The Pathfinder lander bounced to a stop on Mars, cushioned by airbags. Its ramps opened and Sojourner drove down onto the surface. It stayed within range of the lander, which relayed its data to Earth.
reviewNotes: Confirm the date the rover's own operations ended versus the lander's last transmission.

name: Ingenuity Mars Helicopter
statusDetail: Completed 72 flights, far more than the five planned. A rotor blade was damaged on its final flight and NASA ended the mission in January 2024. It remains on the surface of Mars.
purpose: Show that powered, controlled flight is possible in the thin air of Mars.
simpleExplanation: A tiny helicopter that flew in the thin air of Mars, proving that flying on another world is possible.
scientificContribution: Proved that aircraft can fly on Mars and scouted the terrain ahead for the Perseverance rover.
historicalSignificance: The first powered, controlled aircraft to fly on another planet. Its first flight was on April 19, 2021.
modelDescription: A small, boxy body on four thin legs, with two long, narrow rotor blades stacked above it that spin in opposite directions, and a solar panel on top.
audioDescription: Ingenuity is a small, lightweight helicopter with a boxy body held on four thin, spindly legs. Above it, two long, narrow rotor blades spin in opposite directions, one above the other, each about one point two metres across. A small solar panel sits on top, above the blades.
visualExplanation: Ingenuity travelled to Mars attached to the underside of the Perseverance rover. It was lowered to the ground, charged its batteries with its solar panel, and then spun its blades at about 2,400 turns a minute to lift off in Mars's thin air.
reviewNotes: Confirm the flight count and mission end date against NASA's final mission summary.

name: Pioneer 10
statusDetail: NASA ended the formal mission in 1997. The final faint signal was received on January 23, 2003. It is still travelling away from the Sun.
physicalLocation: Outer Solar System, travelling away from the Sun
purpose: Travel through the asteroid belt and past Jupiter to study the outer Solar System.
simpleExplanation: A robot explorer launched in 1972 that flew past Jupiter and kept going, carrying a message plate for anyone who might find it.
scientificContribution: Returned the first close-up views of Jupiter and measured its radiation and magnetic environment.
historicalSignificance: The first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt and the first to fly past Jupiter. It carries a plaque with a message from humanity.
modelDescription: A spacecraft with a large round dish antenna, a six-sided instrument box behind it, two long booms carrying power generators, a third boom with a magnetometer, and a small plaque on the antenna struts.
audioDescription: Pioneer 10 has a large, round, dish-shaped antenna, about two point seven metres wide, that always points back toward Earth. Behind the dish sits a small, six-sided box holding the instruments. Two long arms stretch out to the sides, each holding a power source, and a third arm carries a sensor that measures magnetic fields. A small gold-coloured plaque is fixed to the antenna's support struts.
visualExplanation: Pioneer 10 used its dish to point at Earth and send faint radio signals home. As it passed Jupiter, the planet's gravity flung it onward, faster, out toward the edge of the Solar System.
reviewNotes: Confirm the distinction between formal mission end (1997) and last signal (2003). The team listed this under Mars; it is a deep-space mission.

name: Pioneer 11
statusDetail: Routine operations ended on September 30, 1995 as its power declined. Its final communication was in November 1995. It is still travelling away from the Sun.
physicalLocation: Outer Solar System, travelling away from the Sun
purpose: Fly past Jupiter and Saturn to study the giant planets.
simpleExplanation: A robot explorer that flew past Jupiter and then became the first to visit Saturn, showing its rings up close.
scientificContribution: Flew by Jupiter in December 1974 and Saturn in September 1979, returning close-up images and measurements of the planets, Saturn's rings and their magnetic environments.
historicalSignificance: The first spacecraft to fly past Saturn. Its data helped NASA plan the later Voyager missions.
modelDescription: A spacecraft with a large round dish antenna, a six-sided instrument box behind it, two long booms carrying power generators, a third boom with a magnetometer, and a small plaque on the antenna struts.
modelSource: Pioneer 11 (https://skfb.ly/otrXX) by Danny.Gallegos is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
audioDescription: Pioneer 11 looks very much like its twin, Pioneer 10. It has a large, round, dish-shaped antenna that points back toward Earth. Behind the dish sits a small, six-sided box holding the instruments. Two long arms stretch out to the sides, each holding a power source, and a third arm carries a sensor that measures magnetic fields. A small gold-coloured plaque is fixed to the antenna's support struts.
visualExplanation: Pioneer 11 first flew past Jupiter, and Jupiter's gravity bent its path toward Saturn. It passed close to Saturn's rings, sent back pictures and measurements, then continued out of the planets' region.
reviewNotes: No source link yet: add the official NASA Science and NSSDCA pages. Confirm exact last-contact date and the Voyager claim.
